Lab 1

making decisions · 9 different questions · 3 forms

Lab instructions (as given in lab1a)

Three questions, one file each. Each one reads its input, decides, and prints the answer — nothing more. You need only what is already covered: operator precedence, if/else, switch, and where a variable lives.

This course uses C++17. Build any question with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic q1.cpp -o q1
./q1

Each program reads its input from the keyboard and prints one line.

over-current protectionlab1a q1

Input: current safeLimit stopFlag (a current, the safe limit, and 1 when the emergency stop is pressed, 0 when it is not).

Test the conditions in this order — exceptional case first:

ConditionPrint
the current is negativeINVALID
the emergency stop is pressed, or the current is above safeLimitTRIP
the current is above 90% of safeLimitWARNING
anything elseNORMAL

The order is the whole point. A negative reading is meaningless, so it is reported before anything else is even considered — including the stop button.

Use else if for the middle conditions, so that reaching one means every condition above it was already false. Watch the boundaries: above the limit trips, exactly at it does not.

3 10 0    -> NORMAL
9.5 10 0  -> WARNING
12 10 0   -> TRIP

is it a multiple?lab1a q3

Input: value divisor.

ConditionPrint
divisor is zeroINVALID
value is an exact multiple of divisorDIVISIBLE
anything elseNOT DIVISIBLE

value % divisor is the remainder left after dividing, so a remainder of zero means it divided exactly.

% is undefined when the divisor is zero — the program may do anything at all, including crash. So the zero has to be ruled out before the % is reached. Test it first, or let && stop early:

if (divisor != 0 && value % divisor == 0)

The left side is checked first, and if it is false the right side never runs.

Zero is a multiple of everything, and negative values work the same way — check both against your code rather than guessing.

12 4 -> DIVISIBLE
13 4 -> NOT DIVISIBLE
7 0  -> INVALID

how badly hurt is the actorlab1b q1

Input: hp maxHp.

Test the conditions in this order — exceptional case first:

ConditionPrint
hp is negative, maxHp is not positive, or hp is above maxHpINVALID
hp is zeroDEAD
hp is at most a quarter of maxHpCRITICAL
hp is below maxHpHURT
anything elseFULL

The order is the whole point. Nonsense health is rejected before it can be classified, and once you have ruled out everything above it, "anything else" can only mean full health — the cases are exhaustive.

Both values are whole numbers, so write the quarter test without division: hp * 4 <= maxHp says the same thing and cannot round. * binds tighter than <=, so no brackets are needed there.

100 100 -> FULL
25 100  -> CRITICAL
120 100 -> INVALID

one move on the boardlab1b q2

The board is 5 rows (0 to 4) and 9 columns (0 to 8). There is one obstacle, at row 2, column 4.

Input: row column command, where the command is a single character:

CommandMeans
wup, one row
sdown, one row
aleft, one column
dright, one column
anything elsestay where you are

Use a switch on the command to set dRow and dColumn — how far to move in each direction. Both start at zero, so an unknown command needs no case of its own: the default simply leaves them alone.

Then work out the square the command asks for, and move only if that square is inside the board and is not the obstacle. Otherwise the actor stays put.

Print position = <row>,<column> — no spaces around the comma.

0 0 d -> position = 0,1
0 0 w -> position = 0,0      (off the edge, so no move)
2 3 d -> position = 2,3      (the obstacle is there, so no move)

what happens on this ticklab1b q3

The level does something on some ticks and nothing on the rest: a monster spawns every 3rd tick, a health pickup appears every 5th tick.

Input: tick, one number.

Test the conditions in this order — exceptional case first:

ConditionPrint
tick is negativeINVALID
the tick is a spawn tick and a heal tickBOSS
the tick is a spawn tickSPAWN
the tick is a heal tickHEAL
anything elseQUIET

"Every 3rd tick" is tick % 3 == 0 — the remainder after dividing by 3 is zero. Note that % binds tighter than ==, so that reads as (tick % 3) == 0, which is what you want.

The order is the whole point. Tick 15 is a multiple of both, so if you test tick % 3 == 0 first it will answer SPAWN and you will never reach the BOSS branch. The most specific case has to come first.

15 -> BOSS
9  -> SPAWN
10 -> HEAL
7  -> QUIET

36 different questions · 12 forms

Lab instructions (as given in lab2B1a)

Three questions, one file each. Each one reads its input, works out the answer, and prints it — nothing more. You need only what has been covered so far: operators, if/else, switch, and the while and for loops. No arrays, no functions of your own, no strings.

This course uses C++17. Build any question with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic q1.cpp -o q1
./q1

Each program reads its input from the keyboard and prints one line.

the grade bandmarks, digits and odd numberslab2B1a q1

Input: score, one whole number out of 100.

ConditionPrint
score is below 0 or above 100INVALID
score is at least 90A
score is at least 80B
score is at least 70C
score is at least 60D
anything elseF

How to do it. Reject the impossible score first, before any band is considered. Then walk the bands downwards from the highest one, each test chained to the one above it with else. Because a chained test is only reached when every test above it was false, you never have to write the upper end of a band: reaching the 80 test already means the score was under 90. The final else needs no test at all — everything not caught above is an F.

The arithmetic.

INVALID  when  score < 0  or  score > 100
A  when  90 <= score <= 100
B  when  80 <= score < 90
C  when  70 <= score < 80
D  when  60 <= score < 70
F  when  0 <= score < 60

Worked examples:

95           -> A
80           -> B
65           -> D

adding up the digitsmarks, digits and odd numberslab2B1a q2

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is negativeINVALID
anything elsethe sum of the digits of n

How to do it. A number gives up its digits from the right. The remainder after dividing by ten is the last digit; dividing by ten throws that digit away. Add the last digit to a running total, drop it, and keep going while anything is left. Start the total at zero. Note that zero itself has one digit, so the loop body must run at least once even when the number is already zero — a plain while (n > 0) prints nothing for zero, which is wrong.

The arithmetic.

last digit of n  =  n % 10
n with its last digit removed  =  n / 10      (whole-number division)
sum  =  d0 + d1 + d2 + ...  where  n = d0 + 10*d1 + 100*d2 + ...

Worked examples:

0            -> 0
7            -> 7
123          -> 6

the first odd numbersmarks, digits and odd numberslab2B1a q3

Input: n, how many odd numbers to add.

ConditionPrint
n is below 1INVALID
anything elsethe sum of the first n odd numbers

How to do it. Count a variable from 1 up to n, and on each pass work out which odd number that position stands for and add it to a running total. The first odd number is 1, the second is 3, the third is 5 — each one is two more than the last, so position i holds the value two times i minus one. Keep the running total outside the loop, or it is reset on every pass.

The arithmetic.

i-th odd number  =  2*i - 1
sum  =  1 + 3 + 5 + ... + (2n - 1)
closed form (use it to check your loop)  sum  =  n^2

Worked examples:

1            -> 1
2            -> 4
5            -> 25

what kind of triangletriangles, digit counts and factorialslab2B1b q1

Input: a b c, the three side lengths.

ConditionPrint
the three lengths cannot form a triangleNOT A TRIANGLE
all three sides are equalEQUILATERAL
exactly two sides are equalISOSCELES
anything elseSCALENE

How to do it. Decide whether it is a triangle at all before deciding what kind. Three lengths form a triangle only when every side is positive and each side is shorter than the other two added together — all three of those sums have to be checked, not just one. Once that is settled, compare the sides: all three equal is equilateral, otherwise any one matching pair is isosceles, and if no pair matches it is scalene. Note that the equilateral test has to come first, because all three equal also satisfies 'two are equal'.

The arithmetic.

a triangle needs  a > 0,  b > 0,  c > 0
and  a + b > c,  a + c > b,  b + c > a
equilateral  when  a = b = c
isosceles  when  exactly one of  a = b,  b = c,  a = c  holds

Worked examples:

3 3 3        -> EQUILATERAL
5 5 8        -> ISOSCELES
3 4 5        -> SCALENE

how many digitstriangles, digit counts and factorialslab2B1b q2

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is negativeINVALID
anything elsehow many digits n is written with

How to do it. Strip one digit at a time off the right-hand end and count how many strips it takes to reach nothing. Dividing a whole number by ten removes its last digit. Count the strip first and test afterwards, so that zero — which is written with one digit but is already zero before the loop starts — is counted once rather than not at all.

The arithmetic.

n with its last digit removed  =  n / 10      (whole-number division)
digits(n)  =  1 + digits(n / 10)   for n >= 10,   and  digits(n) = 1  for  0 <= n <= 9

Worked examples:

0            -> 1
7            -> 1
10           -> 2

factorialtriangles, digit counts and factorialslab2B1b q3

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 0 or above 12INVALID
anything elsen factorial

How to do it. Start a running product at one — not at zero, which would swallow everything — and multiply it by each whole number from two up to n in turn. Nothing above the upper limit is asked for, because 13 factorial no longer fits in an int and would silently wrap around to a wrong answer; that is why the range is rejected up front. Zero factorial is one, and the loop handles it for free by never running.

The arithmetic.

n!  =  1 * 2 * 3 * ... * n
0!  =  1
n!  =  n * (n-1)!

Worked examples:

0            -> 1
1            -> 1
5            -> 120

write the number backwardsa calculator, reversal and Fibonaccilab2B1c q2

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is negativeINVALID
anything elsethe digits of n in reverse order

How to do it. Build the answer as a number, not as text. Keep a result that starts at zero. On each pass, push the result one place to the left by multiplying it by ten, and add the last digit of what is left of the input; then drop that digit from the input. The last digit read becomes the leading digit of the result. Trailing zeros in the input simply disappear, because a leading zero is not a digit of a number.

The arithmetic.

last digit  =  n % 10
result  =  result * 10 + (n % 10)
n  =  n / 10      (whole-number division, repeated until n is 0)

Worked examples:

0            -> 0
7            -> 7
123          -> 321

the n-th Fibonacci numbera calculator, reversal and Fibonaccilab2B1c q3

Input: n, which term is wanted (the first term is 1).

ConditionPrint
n is below 1INVALID
anything elsethe n-th Fibonacci number

How to do it. Hold only two numbers, the current term and the one after it, both starting at one. Each pass of the loop slides the pair one step along the sequence: the next term becomes the current one, and their sum becomes the new next term. Run the slide one time fewer than n, because the pair already starts at the first term. Use a third variable to hold the sum while you overwrite the other two, or you lose a value mid-swap.

The arithmetic.

F(1) = 1,  F(2) = 1
F(k)  =  F(k-1) + F(k-2)   for  k >= 3

Worked examples:

1            -> 1
2            -> 1
7            -> 13

is it a leap yearleap years, the Collatz walk and multipleslab2B2a q1

Input: year, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
year is below 1INVALID
year divides exactly by 400LEAP
year divides exactly by 100NOT LEAP
year divides exactly by 4LEAP
anything elseNOT LEAP

How to do it. The rules overlap, so the order they are tested in decides the answer. Test the most specific rule first and chain the rest below it with else: 400 before 100, and 100 before 4. Written that way each test is only reached when the ones above it failed, so no test needs to repeat what was already ruled out. Divides exactly means the remainder after division is zero.

The arithmetic.

divides exactly  when  year % k = 0
LEAP      when  year % 400 = 0
NOT LEAP  when  year % 100 = 0  and  year % 400 != 0
LEAP      when  year % 4 = 0  and  year % 100 != 0

Worked examples:

2000         -> LEAP
1900         -> NOT LEAP
2024         -> LEAP

the Collatz walkleap years, the Collatz walk and multipleslab2B2a q2

Input: n, the starting number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 1INVALID
anything elsehow many steps it takes to reach 1

How to do it. Keep changing the number until it becomes one, counting each change. The rule depends on the number each time round, so the branch lives inside the loop: an even number is halved, an odd one is tripled and increased by one. A number that is already one takes no steps at all, which a while gives you for free by not running. Do not attempt to predict the number of steps — the count does not rise smoothly with the starting value.

The arithmetic.

n is even  when  n % 2 = 0
next  =  n / 2        when n is even
next  =  3*n + 1      when n is odd
stop when  n = 1

Worked examples:

1            -> 0
2            -> 1
3            -> 7

counting multiplesleap years, the Collatz walk and multipleslab2B2a q3

Input: n k, the upper limit and the divisor.

ConditionPrint
n is below 1 or k is below 1INVALID
anything elsehow many numbers from 1 to n are exact multiples of k

How to do it. Rule out the nonsense inputs first, in particular a divisor of zero: taking a remainder by zero is undefined and may crash. Then count from one up to n and add one to a tally whenever the current number leaves no remainder when divided by k. Whole-number division gives the same answer straight away, which makes a good check on the loop you wrote.

The arithmetic.

i is a multiple of k  when  i % k = 0
count  =  how many i in 1..n satisfy that
closed form (use it to check your loop)  count  =  n / k   (whole-number division)

Worked examples:

10 3         -> 3
10 1         -> 10
7 8          -> 0

stop when  n = 1
the answer is the largest k with  2^k <= n

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 2INVALID
anything elsethe largest divisor of n that is smaller than n itself

How to do it. Every number above one has at least one such divisor, because one always divides it. Count downwards from one below n and stop at the first number that divides n exactly — counting down means the first one found is already the largest, so nothing more needs to be compared. A for loop may count down as easily as up; the step is what changes. A prime number gives one, since nothing between them divides it.

The arithmetic.

d divides n  when  n % d = 0
answer  =  the largest d with  1 <= d < n  and  n % d = 0
for a prime n the answer is 1

9            -> 3
12           -> 6

sign and paritysigns, common divisors and primeslab2B3a q1

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is zeroZERO
n is above zero and evenPOSITIVE EVEN
n is above zero and oddPOSITIVE ODD
n is below zero and evenNEGATIVE EVEN
anything elseNEGATIVE ODD

How to do it. Two independent facts are being reported, so handle them as two decisions rather than four unrelated ones: first take zero out of the way, because it is neither positive nor negative; then decide the sign; and inside each sign, decide the parity. Nesting the parity test inside the sign test means each test is written once. Take care with the remainder of a negative number — in C++ it may come out negative, so testing whether the remainder equals one misses the odd negatives. Test against zero instead, which is safe for both signs.

The arithmetic.

n is even  when  n % 2 = 0
n is odd   when  n % 2 != 0      (do not test n % 2 = 1: for negative n it can be -1)
sign:  n > 0 positive,  n < 0 negative,  n = 0 neither

Worked examples:

0            -> ZERO
4            -> POSITIVE EVEN
7            -> POSITIVE ODD

the greatest common divisorsigns, common divisors and primeslab2B3a q2

Input: a b, two whole numbers.

ConditionPrint
a or b is below 1INVALID
anything elsethe greatest common divisor of a and b

How to do it. Use repeated subtraction. While the two numbers differ, take the smaller away from the larger and keep both; the pair shrinks but shares exactly the divisors it started with. When they finally meet, that common value is the greatest common divisor. The branch that decides which one to subtract from lives inside the loop. Equal numbers are already the answer, so the loop must be able to run zero times.

The arithmetic.

gcd(a, a)  =  a
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a - b, b)   when  a > b
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a, b - a)   when  b > a
stop when  a = b

Worked examples:

12 18        -> 6
7 13         -> 1
100 75       -> 25

How to do it. Try every possible divisor from two up to one below n, and remember whether any of them divided exactly. Use a flag variable set before the loop and cleared the moment a divisor is found; decide what to print after the loop has finished, from the flag. Printing inside the loop is the common mistake — a number with several divisors then prints several lines. Two is prime, and it works out correctly here because the loop never runs for it.

d divides n  when  n % d = 0
n is prime  when no d with  2 <= d <= n - 1  divides n
1 and everything below it are neither prime nor composite

9            -> NOT PRIME

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 1INVALID
the divisors below n add up to exactly nPERFECT
they add up to more than nABUNDANT
anything elseDEFICIENT

How to do it. Add up every divisor of n that is smaller than n itself, then compare that total against n. The loop only sums; the decision happens after it, once, on the finished total. n itself must be left out of the sum, which is what the upper limit of the loop takes care of. One has no divisor below it, so its total is zero and it comes out deficient.

The arithmetic.

d is a proper divisor of n  when  n % d = 0  and  1 <= d < n
s  =  the sum of all proper divisors of n
PERFECT when s = n,   ABUNDANT when s > n,   DEFICIENT when s < n

8            -> DEFICIENT

Input: a series of whole numbers, ending with 0.

ConditionPrint
no number arrived before the 0NONE
anything elsethe largest of the numbers read before the 0

How to do it. The count of numbers is not known in advance, which is exactly when a while earns its place over a for: the loop is driven by what it reads, not by a counter. Read one number at a time and stop as soon as the stopping value arrives; that value is a marker, not data, so it never takes part in the comparison. Keep the largest seen so far in a variable, replacing it whenever a bigger one turns up, and keep a separate flag or count for whether anything was read at all. Do not start the largest at zero — every reading may be negative, and zero would then win a contest it was never entered in. Start it from the first number actually read instead.

The arithmetic.

stop as soon as the value read equals 0
largest  =  value  whenever  value > largest
with no values read at all, the answer is NONE

3 9 4 0      -> 9
-5 -2 0      -> -2
7 0          -> 7

how many real rootsroots, palindromes and split sumslab2B4a q1

Input: a b c, the three coefficients.

ConditionPrint
a is zeroNOT QUADRATIC
the discriminant is above zeroTWO ROOTS
the discriminant is zeroONE ROOT
anything elseNO REAL ROOTS

How to do it. The leading coefficient being zero has to be caught first: without it the equation is not quadratic at all, and the usual reasoning does not apply. Then compute the discriminant once into its own variable and branch on its sign. The roots themselves are not asked for, so no square root is needed anywhere — only the sign of that one value decides the answer.

The arithmetic.

equation:  a*x^2 + b*x + c = 0
discriminant  D  =  b^2 - 4*a*c
D > 0  two distinct real roots
D = 0  one repeated real root
D < 0  no real roots
a = 0  not a quadratic equation

Worked examples:

1 -3 2       -> TWO ROOTS
1 2 1        -> ONE ROOT
1 0 5        -> NO REAL ROOTS

Input: n, one whole number.

anything elseNOT PALINDROME

How to do it. Build the reverse of the number the same way as before — push a result left by a factor of ten and add the last digit of what remains — and then compare the finished reverse with the original. Keep a copy of the original before the loop starts, because the loop destroys the number it is reading. A single digit is always a palindrome, and the loop gives that answer without any special case.

The arithmetic.

reverse  =  reverse * 10 + (n % 10),   then  n = n / 10,   repeated until n is 0
n is a palindrome  when  reverse = original n

121          -> PALINDROME
123          -> NOT PALINDROME
7            -> PALINDROME

weekday or weekenddays of the week, growing totals and serieslab2B4c q1

Input: day, a day number where 1 is Monday.

ConditionPrint
day is 1 to 5WEEKDAY
day is 6 or 7WEEKEND
anything elseINVALID DAY

How to do it. Use a switch on the day number. Five labels stacked in front of one body give the weekdays and two give the weekend, so the whole week is three statements rather than seven. Each group still ends with its own break, and the default catches a day number outside the week — including zero, which is a natural typing mistake when the days are numbered from one.

The arithmetic.

WEEKDAY:  day in {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}
WEEKEND:  day in {6, 7}
valid days are  1 <= day <= 7

Worked examples:

1            -> WEEKDAY
5            -> WEEKDAY
6            -> WEEKEND

how many terms until it overflowsdays of the week, growing totals and serieslab2B4c q2

Input: limit, the total to exceed.

ConditionPrint
limit is negativeINVALID
anything elsehow many of 1, 2, 3, ... have to be added before the total passes limit

How to do it. Add the whole numbers one after another into a running total, counting them, and stop as soon as the total is strictly greater than the limit. The stopping point depends on the total, which is not known in advance, so the loop is a while on the total rather than a for over a fixed count. Strictly greater is the requirement: a total that merely equals the limit has not passed it, so one more term is still needed. A limit of zero already needs one term, because the empty total of zero does not pass it.

The arithmetic.

after k terms the total is  1 + 2 + ... + k  =  k*(k + 1) / 2
answer  =  the smallest k with  k*(k + 1) / 2  >  limit

Worked examples:

0            -> 1
1            -> 2
5            -> 3

the n-th term of the seriesdays of the week, growing totals and serieslab2B4c q3

Input: a d n, the first term, the common difference and which term is wanted.

ConditionPrint
n is below 1INVALID
anything elsethe n-th term of the series

How to do it. Start at the first term and step forward by the common difference, one step per pass, doing one step fewer than n because the first term is where you already are. A difference of zero and a negative difference both work with no special handling — the same step is simply taken with a different value. The closed form is there to check the loop against, not to replace it.

The arithmetic.

terms:  a,  a + d,  a + 2d,  a + 3d,  ...
closed form (use it to check your loop)  term(n)  =  a + (n - 1)*d

Worked examples:

2 3 4        -> 11
5 0 10       -> 5
0 -2 3       -> -4

Lab 3

64 different questions · 16 forms

Lab instructions (as given in lab3B1a)

Four questions, one file each. This lab is about functions: every answer has to be worked out inside a function you declare and define yourself. You need only what lecture 7 covered, plus the operators, if/else and loops you have already used. No arrays, no strings, no reference parameters.

This course uses C++17. Build any question with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic q1.cpp -o q1
./q1

Each program reads its input from the keyboard and prints one line.

Every question here is about writing a function. For each one you must:

  1. declare it above main — the prototype, ending in a semicolon;
  2. define it below main — the same signature, followed by the body;
  3. call it from main.

check.sh looks for the declaration and the definition separately. A program that computes the right answer inside main scores nothing.

The arithmetic.

area = length * width

a triangular tile patternrectangles and tileslab3B1a q4
int rowArea(int tiles, int tileSide);
int patternArea(int rows, int tileSide);

Input: rows tileSide.

ConditionPrint
either number is less than 1INVALID
anything elsethe total area of the pattern

How to do it. The pattern is triangular: row 1 holds one square tile, row 2 holds two, row 3 holds three, and so on down to the last row. rowArea gives the area of a single row — a count of tiles times the area of one tile. patternArea runs a loop counting the rows from 1 upwards, calls rowArea on each pass, and adds each answer into a running total it returns at the end. Keep the total outside the loop, or it resets every pass. Note that main calls patternArea only: the call to rowArea happens inside it. Multiplying instead of looping gives the wrong answer, because each row holds a different number of tiles.

The arithmetic.

area of one tile   = tileSide * tileSide
area of row k      = k * tileSide * tileSide
total for r rows   = (1 + 2 + ... + r) * tileSide * tileSide

Worked examples:

1 2                  -> 4
3 2                  -> 24
2 5                  -> 75
0 5                  -> INVALID
3 0                  -> INVALID

a week of growing salesa shopping billlab3B2a q4
int itemTotal(int quantity, int unitPrice);
int weekTakings(int days, int unitPrice);

Input: days unitPrice.

ConditionPrint
days is less than 1, or the unit price is negativeINVALID
anything elsethe takings over all the days

How to do it. Sales grow by one item a day: one is sold on day 1, two on day 2, three on day 3, all at the same unit price. weekTakings runs a loop counting the days from 1 upwards, calls itemTotal on each pass for that day's sales, and adds the answers into a running total it returns at the end. Keep the total outside the loop, or it resets every pass. main calls weekTakings only — the call to itemTotal happens inside it. Because a different number is sold each day, multiplying one day's takings by the number of days gives the wrong answer.

The arithmetic.

takings on day k = k * unitPrice
total over d days = (1 + 2 + ... + d) * unitPrice

5 2                  -> 30
0 10                 -> INVALID
3 -1                 -> INVALID

packing the consignmentsweights and packinglab3B3c q4
int boxesNeeded(int items, int perBox);
int totalBoxes(int consignments, int perBox);

Input: consignments perBox.

ConditionPrint
consignments is less than 1, or perBox is less than 1INVALID
anything elsethe total number of boxes

How to do it. Consignment k holds k items — the first holds one, the second two, and so on. boxesNeeded rounds up, because leftover items still need a box of their own; the arithmetic below does that without a loop. totalBoxes loops over the consignments, calls boxesNeeded for each, and adds the boxes up. Each consignment is packed on its own, so each one rounds up separately — which is why this is not the same as adding all the items together and rounding once at the end.

The arithmetic.

boxes for one consignment = (items + perBox - 1) / perBox
consignment k holds k items

Worked examples:

1 5                  -> 1
3 5                  -> 3
6 3                  -> 9
10 1                 -> 55
0 5                  -> INVALID

rows to fill or seats to spareexam halls and seatinglab3B4d q3
int rowsNeeded(int students, int seatsPerRow);
int seatsLeftOver(int students, int seatsPerRow);

Input: code students seatsPerRow.

ConditionPrint
code is not 1 or 2, students is negative, or seatsPerRow is less than 1INVALID
code is 1the rows needed
code is 2the empty seats in the last row

How to do it. A part-filled row is still a row, so rowsNeeded rounds up — the arithmetic below does that without a loop and without a branch. seatsLeftOver asks the other half of the same question: how many seats in that last row go unused. When the students fill the rows exactly, nothing is left over, and the second % seatsPerRow is what turns a full row of spare seats into 0.

The arithmetic.

rows needed = (students + seatsPerRow - 1) / seatsPerRow
left over   = (seatsPerRow - students % seatsPerRow) % seatsPerRow

Worked examples:

1 100 12             -> 9
2 100 12             -> 8
1 24 12              -> 2
3 100 12             -> INVALID
1 100 0              -> INVALID

Lab 4

references, recursion and arrays · 64 different questions · 16 forms

Lab instructions (as given in lab4B1a)

Four questions, one file each. This lab covers lectures 8 and 9: reference parameters, recursion, and fixed-size arrays with their count passed beside them. Everything else — operators, if/else, loops, value parameters — you have already used. No std::vector, no strings.

This course uses C++17. Build any question with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic q1.cpp -o q1
./q1

Each program reads its input from the keyboard and prints one line.

Every question is about writing a function. For each one you must:

  1. declare it above main — the prototype, ending in a semicolon;
  2. define it below main — the same signature, followed by the body;
  3. call it from main.

check.sh looks for the declaration and the definition separately, and for the shape the question asks for: q1 and q4 must use a & reference parameter, q2 must not contain for or while, q3 and q4 must loop. A program that computes the right answer some other way scores nothing.

In q3 and q4 the template already reads the input into int values[10] and the number of entries into count; a C-style array does not know its own size, so the function takes count as a parameter and loops up to it, never to 10.

a run timerlab4B1a q1

A running app records the whole run in seconds and shows minutes and seconds.

void splitSeconds(int total, int& minutes, int& seconds);

Input: total

ConditionPrint
total is negativeINVALID
anything elseminutes seconds, one space between

How to do it. The function returns nothing: its two answers go back through the reference parameters. main declares two int variables, passes them as the last two arguments, and after the call prints them. The & in the prototype and the definition is what lets the function write into main's variables.

The arithmetic.

minutes = total / 60
seconds = total % 60

Worked examples:

125                  -> 2 5
3600                 -> 60 0
59                   -> 0 59
0                    -> 0 0
-5                   -> INVALID

the sum of the digitslab4B1a q2

A checksum adds every digit of a number together.

int digitSum(int n);

Input: n

ConditionPrint
n is negativeINVALID
anything elsethe sum of its digits

How to do it. No loop is allowed in this file — check.sh rejects for and while. The function calls itself: the last digit is n % 10, and the rest of the number is n / 10, which is a smaller problem of the same kind. The base case is n being 0, whose digit sum is 0. main checks the sign and prints the returned value.

The arithmetic.

digitSum(0) = 0
digitSum(n) = n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10)

1234                 -> 10

1000                 -> 1
0                    -> 0
-12                  -> INVALID

the greatest common divisorlab4B2d q2

A fraction simplifier needs the greatest common divisor of two numbers.

int gcd(int a, int b);

Input: a b

ConditionPrint
either number is less than 1INVALID
anything elsethe greatest common divisor

How to do it. Euclid's rule, recursively: the gcd of a and b is the gcd of b and a % b, and when b reaches 0 the answer is a. That last line is the base case. No loop in this file. main checks both inputs are at least 1.

The arithmetic.

gcd(a, 0) = a
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)

Input: a b

ConditionPrint

anything elsethe greatest common divisor

How to do it. Euclid's rule, recursively: the gcd of a and b is the gcd of b and a % b, and when b reaches 0 the answer is a. That last line is the base case. No loop in this file. main checks both inputs are at least 1.

gcd(a, 0) = a
gcd(a, b) = gcd(b, a % b)

Lab 5

bug finding · 48 different questions · 8 forms

Lab instructions (as given in lab5Ba)

Six programs, one file each. Every one of them is a complete program for a question from an earlier lab (labs 1 to 4), and every one of them has exactly one bug. The program compiles; it just prints the wrong thing for some inputs.

Your job for each question:

  1. read what the program is supposed to print, below;
  2. run it, compare with the worked examples, and find the line that is wrong;
  3. fix it with the smallest change that makes it correct — usually one line.

Do not rewrite the program. The TAs grade the diff between the file you were given and the file you push: a correct answer that replaces the program scores nothing, because the question is whether you can find the bug, not whether you can solve the original lab again. Keep the function names, the structure and the output format exactly as they are.

This course uses C++17. Build any question with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic q1.cpp -o q1
./q1

Each program reads its input from the keyboard and prints one line. The compiler warnings from -Wall -Wextra are worth reading: they point at some of the bugs.

over-current protection (from Lab 1)lab5Ba q1

Input: current safeLimit stopFlag (a current, the safe limit, and 1 when the emergency stop is pressed, 0 when it is not).

Test the conditions in this order — exceptional case first:

ConditionPrint
the current is negativeINVALID
the emergency stop is pressed, or the current is above safeLimitTRIP
the current is above 90% of safeLimitWARNING
anything elseNORMAL

The order is the whole point. A negative reading is meaningless, so it is reported before anything else is even considered — including the stop button.

Use else if for the middle conditions, so that reaching one means every condition above it was already false. Watch the boundaries: above the limit trips, exactly at it does not.

3 10 0    -> NORMAL
9.5 10 0  -> WARNING
12 10 0   -> TRIP
Starter file q1.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Ba, question 1: over-current protection (from Lab 1)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    double current = 0.0;
    double safeLimit = 0.0;
    int stopFlag = 0;
    std::cin >> current >> safeLimit >> stopFlag;

    if (current < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else if (stopFlag == 1 || current >= safeLimit) {
        std::cout << "TRIP" << '\n';
    } else if (current > 0.9 * safeLimit) {
        std::cout << "WARNING" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "NORMAL" << '\n';
    }
}
what kind of triangle (from Lab 2)lab5Ba q2

Input: a b c, the three side lengths.

ConditionPrint
the three lengths cannot form a triangleNOT A TRIANGLE
all three sides are equalEQUILATERAL
exactly two sides are equalISOSCELES
anything elseSCALENE

How to do it. Decide whether it is a triangle at all before deciding what kind. Three lengths form a triangle only when every side is positive and each side is shorter than the other two added together — all three of those sums have to be checked, not just one. Once that is settled, compare the sides: all three equal is equilateral, otherwise any one matching pair is isosceles, and if no pair matches it is scalene. Note that the equilateral test has to come first, because all three equal also satisfies 'two are equal'.

The arithmetic.

a triangle needs  a > 0,  b > 0,  c > 0
and  a + b > c,  a + c > b,  b + c > a
equilateral  when  a = b = c
isosceles  when  exactly one of  a = b,  b = c,  a = c  holds

Worked examples:

3 3 3        -> EQUILATERAL
5 5 8        -> ISOSCELES
3 4 5        -> SCALENE
Starter file q2.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Ba, question 2: what kind of triangle (from Lab 2)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 0;
    int b = 0;
    int c = 0;
    std::cin >> a >> b >> c;

    if (a <= 0 || b <= 0 || c <= 0 || a + b < c || a + c <= b || b + c <= a) {
        std::cout << "NOT A TRIANGLE" << '\n';
    } else if (a == b && b == c) {
        std::cout << "EQUILATERAL" << '\n';
    } else if (a == b || b == c || a == c) {
        std::cout << "ISOSCELES" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "SCALENE" << '\n';
    }
}
is it prime (from Lab 2)lab5Ba q3

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 2INVALID
n has a divisor other than 1 and itselfNOT PRIME
anything elsePRIME

How to do it. Try every possible divisor from two up to one below n, and remember whether any of them divided exactly. Use a flag variable set before the loop and cleared the moment a divisor is found; decide what to print after the loop has finished, from the flag. Printing inside the loop is the common mistake — a number with several divisors then prints several lines. Two is prime, and it works out correctly here because the loop never runs for it.

The arithmetic.

d divides n  when  n % d = 0
n is prime  when no d with  2 <= d <= n - 1  divides n
1 and everything below it are neither prime nor composite

Worked examples:

2            -> PRIME
9            -> NOT PRIME
97           -> PRIME
Starter file q3.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Ba, question 3: is it prime (from Lab 2)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 2) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }

    bool prime = true;
    for (int d = 2; d <= n; ++d) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            prime = false;
        }
    }

    if (prime) {
        std::cout << "PRIME" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "NOT PRIME" << '\n';
    }
}
is that a real time? (from Lab 3)lab5Ba q4
bool isValidTime(int hours, int minutes);

Input: hours minutes.

ConditionPrint

anything elseNO

How to do it. This is the one question in the lab with no INVALID — every pair of numbers gets a YES or a NO, because judging the input is the question. A 24-hour clock runs from 0 to 23 hours and 0 to 59 minutes, and all four of those ends are worth testing. Join the four conditions with && and return the result.

Worked examples:

12 30                -> YES
23 59                -> YES
24 0                 -> NO
12 60                -> NO
-1 30                -> NO
Starter file q4.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Ba, question 4: is that a real time? (from Lab 3)

// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

bool isValidTime(int hours, int minutes);

int main() {
    int hours = 0;
    int minutes = 0;
    std::cin >> hours >> minutes;

    if (isValidTime(hours, minutes)) {
        std::cout << "YES" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "NO" << '\n';
    }
}

bool isValidTime(int hours, int minutes) {
    return hours >= 0 && hours <= 24 && minutes >= 0 && minutes <= 59;
}
a pyramid of cubes (from Lab 3)lab5Ba q5
int cubeVolume(int side);
int stackVolume(int n);

Input: n.

ConditionPrint
n is less than 1INVALID
anything elsethe total volume of the stack

How to do it. The stack is a pyramid of n cubes: the one on top has side 1, the next has side 2, and the one at the bottom has side n. stackVolume runs a loop counting from 1 to n, calls cubeVolume for each cube, and adds the volumes into a running total. main calls stackVolume only — the call to cubeVolume happens inside the loop.

The arithmetic.

volume of cube k = k * k * k
total for n      = 1*1*1 + 2*2*2 + ... + n*n*n

Worked examples:

1                    -> 1
2                    -> 9
3                    -> 36
5                    -> 225
0                    -> INVALID
Starter file q5.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Ba, question 5: a pyramid of cubes (from Lab 3)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int cubeVolume(int side);
int stackVolume(int n);

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 1) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << stackVolume(n) << '\n';
    }
}

int cubeVolume(int side) {
    return side * side;
}

int stackVolume(int n) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int k = 1; k <= n; ++k) {
        total = total + cubeVolume(k);
    }
    return total;
}
the length of a song (from Lab 4)lab5Ba q6

A music player stores every track in seconds and shows minutes and seconds.

void splitSeconds(int total, int& minutes, int& seconds);

Input: total

ConditionPrint
total is negativeINVALID
anything elseminutes seconds, one space between

How to do it. The function returns nothing: its two answers go back through the reference parameters. main declares two int variables, passes them as the last two arguments, and after the call prints them. The & in the prototype and the definition is what lets the function write into main's variables.

The arithmetic.

minutes = total / 60
seconds = total % 60

Worked examples:

125                  -> 2 5
3600                 -> 60 0
59                   -> 0 59
0                    -> 0 0
-5                   -> INVALID
Starter file q6.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Ba, question 6: the length of a song (from Lab 4)

// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

void splitSeconds(int total, int minutes, int seconds);

int main() {
    int total = 0;
    std::cin >> total;

    if (total < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }

    int minutes = 0;
    int seconds = 0;
    splitSeconds(total, minutes, seconds);
    std::cout << minutes << ' ' << seconds << '\n';
}

void splitSeconds(int total, int minutes, int seconds) {
    minutes = total / 60;
    seconds = total % 60;
}
is it a multiple? (from Lab 1)lab5Bb q1

Input: value divisor.

ConditionPrint
divisor is zeroINVALID
value is an exact multiple of divisorDIVISIBLE
anything elseNOT DIVISIBLE

value % divisor is the remainder left after dividing, so a remainder of zero means it divided exactly.

% is undefined when the divisor is zero — the program may do anything at all, including crash. So the zero has to be ruled out before the % is reached. Test it first, or let && stop early:

if (divisor != 0 && value % divisor == 0)

The left side is checked first, and if it is false the right side never runs.

Zero is a multiple of everything, and negative values work the same way — check both against your code rather than guessing.

12 4 -> DIVISIBLE
13 4 -> NOT DIVISIBLE
7 0  -> INVALID
Starter file q1.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bb, question 1: is it a multiple? (from Lab 1)

// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int value = 0;
    int divisor = 0;
    std::cin >> value >> divisor;

    if (value == 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else if (value % divisor == 0) {
        std::cout << "DIVISIBLE" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "NOT DIVISIBLE" << '\n';
    }
}
the greatest common divisor (from Lab 2)lab5Bb q2

Input: a b, two whole numbers.

ConditionPrint
a or b is below 1INVALID
anything elsethe greatest common divisor of a and b

How to do it. Use repeated subtraction. While the two numbers differ, take the smaller away from the larger and keep both; the pair shrinks but shares exactly the divisors it started with. When they finally meet, that common value is the greatest common divisor. The branch that decides which one to subtract from lives inside the loop. Equal numbers are already the answer, so the loop must be able to run zero times.

The arithmetic.

gcd(a, a)  =  a
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a - b, b)   when  a > b
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a, b - a)   when  b > a
stop when  a = b

Worked examples:

12 18        -> 6
7 13         -> 1
100 75       -> 25
Starter file q2.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bb, question 2: the greatest common divisor (from Lab 2)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 0;
    int b = 0;
    std::cin >> a >> b;

    if (a < 1 || b < 1) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }

    while (a > b) {
        if (a > b) {
            a = a - b;
        } else {
            b = b - a;
        }
    }
    std::cout << a << '\n';
}
factorial (from Lab 2)lab5Bb q3

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 0 or above 12INVALID
anything elsen factorial

How to do it. Start a running product at one — not at zero, which would swallow everything — and multiply it by each whole number from two up to n in turn. Nothing above the upper limit is asked for, because 13 factorial no longer fits in an int and would silently wrap around to a wrong answer; that is why the range is rejected up front. Zero factorial is one, and the loop handles it for free by never running.

The arithmetic.

n!  =  1 * 2 * 3 * ... * n
0!  =  1
n!  =  n * (n-1)!

Worked examples:

0            -> 1
1            -> 1
5            -> 120

adding up a roll number's digits (from Lab 4)lab5Bb q5

A quick check adds all the digits of an id number together.

int digitSum(int n);

Input: n

ConditionPrint
n is negativeINVALID
anything elsethe sum of its digits

How to do it. No loop is allowed in this file — check.sh rejects for and while. The function calls itself: the last digit is n % 10, and the rest of the number is n / 10, which is a smaller problem of the same kind. The base case is n being 0, whose digit sum is 0. main checks the sign and prints the returned value.

The arithmetic.

digitSum(0) = 0
digitSum(n) = n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10)

Worked examples:

1234                 -> 10
9                    -> 9
1000                 -> 1
0                    -> 0
-12                  -> INVALID
Starter file q5.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bb, question 5: adding up a roll number's digits (from Lab 4)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int digitSum(int n);

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << digitSum(n) << '\n';
    }
}

int digitSum(int n) {
    if (n == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    return n % 10 + digitSum(n / 100);
}
evens and odds (from Lab 4)lab5Bb q6

Ticket numbers are typed in; how many are even and how many odd?

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

Input: count followed by count whole numbers. count is between 1 and 10; the template already reads everything into int values[10] and rejects a bad count.

ConditionPrint
count is not 1 to 10INVALID
anything elseeven odd, one space between

How to do it. Two counters come back through the reference parameters, so the function must set both to 0 before the loop — it cannot assume main did. Then one pass over count elements, adding to one counter or the other. main prints the two variables afterwards.

The arithmetic.

even = number of values with values[i] % 2 == 0
odd  = count - even

Worked examples:

6 12 7 8 15 20 3     -> 3 3
3 1 3 5              -> 0 3
4 2 4 6 8            -> 4 0
1 0                  -> 1 0
11 2 4               -> INVALID

// IC151 — lab5Bb, question 6: evens and odds (from Lab 4)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

int main() {
    int count = 0;
    std::cin >> count;
    if (count < 1 || count > 10) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }
    int values[10] = {};
    for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        std::cin >> values[i];
    }

    int even = 0;
    int odd = 0;
    countEvenOdd(values, count, even, odd);
    std::cout << even << ' ' << odd << '\n';
}

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd) {
    even = 0;
    odd = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < 10; ++i) {
        if (values[i] % 2 == 0) {
            ++even;
        } else {
            ++odd;
        }
    }
}

and  a + b > c,  a + c > b,  b + c > a
equilateral  when  a = b = c
isosceles  when  exactly one of  a = b,  b = c,  a = c  holds

3 4 5        -> SCALENE

is it prime (from Lab 2)lab5Bc q3

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 2INVALID
n has a divisor other than 1 and itselfNOT PRIME
anything elsePRIME

How to do it. Try every possible divisor from two up to one below n, and remember whether any of them divided exactly. Use a flag variable set before the loop and cleared the moment a divisor is found; decide what to print after the loop has finished, from the flag. Printing inside the loop is the common mistake — a number with several divisors then prints several lines. Two is prime, and it works out correctly here because the loop never runs for it.

The arithmetic.

d divides n  when  n % d = 0
n is prime  when no d with  2 <= d <= n - 1  divides n
1 and everything below it are neither prime nor composite

Worked examples:

2            -> PRIME
9            -> NOT PRIME
97           -> PRIME
Starter file q3.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bc, question 3: is it prime (from Lab 2)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 2) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }

    bool prime = true;
    for (int d = 2; d < n; ++d) {
        prime = true;
        if (n % d == 0) {
            prime = false;
        }
    }

    if (prime) {
        std::cout << "PRIME" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "NOT PRIME" << '\n';
    }
}

a pyramid of cubes (from Lab 3)lab5Bc q5
int cubeVolume(int side);
int stackVolume(int n);

Input: n.

ConditionPrint
n is less than 1INVALID
anything elsethe total volume of the stack

How to do it. The stack is a pyramid of n cubes: the one on top has side 1, the next has side 2, and the one at the bottom has side n. stackVolume runs a loop counting from 1 to n, calls cubeVolume for each cube, and adds the volumes into a running total. main calls stackVolume only — the call to cubeVolume happens inside the loop.

The arithmetic.

volume of cube k = k * k * k
total for n      = 1*1*1 + 2*2*2 + ... + n*n*n

Worked examples:

1                    -> 1
2                    -> 9
3                    -> 36
5                    -> 225
0                    -> INVALID
Starter file q5.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bc, question 5: a pyramid of cubes (from Lab 3)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int cubeVolume(int side);
int stackVolume(int n);

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 1) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << stackVolume(n) << '\n';
    }
}

int cubeVolume(int side) {
    return side * side * side;
}

int stackVolume(int n) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int k = 1; k < n; ++k) {
        total = total + cubeVolume(k);
    }
    return total;
}

void splitSeconds(int total, int& minutes, int& seconds);

Input: total

ConditionPrint
total is negativeINVALID
anything elseminutes seconds, one space between

How to do it. The function returns nothing: its two answers go back through the reference parameters. main declares two int variables, passes them as the last two arguments, and after the call prints them. The & in the prototype and the definition is what lets the function write into main's variables.

The arithmetic.

minutes = total / 60
seconds = total % 60

        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;

    int minutes = 0;
    int seconds = 0;

    std::cout << minutes << ' ' << seconds << '\n';
}

void splitSeconds(int total, int& minutes, int& seconds) {
    minutes = total % 60;
    seconds = total / 60;
}
is it a multiple? (from Lab 1)lab5Bd q1

Input: value divisor.

ConditionPrint
divisor is zeroINVALID
value is an exact multiple of divisorDIVISIBLE
anything elseNOT DIVISIBLE

value % divisor is the remainder left after dividing, so a remainder of zero means it divided exactly.

% is undefined when the divisor is zero — the program may do anything at all, including crash. So the zero has to be ruled out before the % is reached. Test it first, or let && stop early:

if (divisor != 0 && value % divisor == 0)

The left side is checked first, and if it is false the right side never runs.

Zero is a multiple of everything, and negative values work the same way — check both against your code rather than guessing.

12 4 -> DIVISIBLE
13 4 -> NOT DIVISIBLE
7 0  -> INVALID

        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else if (value / divisor == 0) {
        std::cout << "DIVISIBLE" << '\n';
    } else {

    }
}
the greatest common divisor (from Lab 2)lab5Bd q2

Input: a b, two whole numbers.

ConditionPrint
a or b is below 1INVALID
anything elsethe greatest common divisor of a and b

How to do it. Use repeated subtraction. While the two numbers differ, take the smaller away from the larger and keep both; the pair shrinks but shares exactly the divisors it started with. When they finally meet, that common value is the greatest common divisor. The branch that decides which one to subtract from lives inside the loop. Equal numbers are already the answer, so the loop must be able to run zero times.

The arithmetic.

gcd(a, a)  =  a
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a - b, b)   when  a > b
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a, b - a)   when  b > a
stop when  a = b

Worked examples:

12 18        -> 6
7 13         -> 1
100 75       -> 25
Starter file q2.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bd, question 2: the greatest common divisor (from Lab 2)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 0;
    int b = 0;
    std::cin >> a >> a;

    if (a < 1 || b < 1) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }

    while (a != b) {
        if (a > b) {
            a = a - b;
        } else {
            b = b - a;
        }
    }
    std::cout << a << '\n';
}
factorial (from Lab 2)lab5Bd q3

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 0 or above 12INVALID
anything elsen factorial

How to do it. Start a running product at one — not at zero, which would swallow everything — and multiply it by each whole number from two up to n in turn. Nothing above the upper limit is asked for, because 13 factorial no longer fits in an int and would silently wrap around to a wrong answer; that is why the range is rejected up front. Zero factorial is one, and the loop handles it for free by never running.

The arithmetic.

n!  =  1 * 2 * 3 * ... * n
0!  =  1
n!  =  n * (n-1)!

Worked examples:

0            -> 1
1            -> 1
5            -> 120

adding up a roll number's digits (from Lab 4)lab5Bd q5

A quick check adds all the digits of an id number together.

int digitSum(int n);

Input: n

ConditionPrint
n is negativeINVALID
anything elsethe sum of its digits

How to do it. No loop is allowed in this file — check.sh rejects for and while. The function calls itself: the last digit is n % 10, and the rest of the number is n / 10, which is a smaller problem of the same kind. The base case is n being 0, whose digit sum is 0. main checks the sign and prints the returned value.

The arithmetic.

digitSum(0) = 0
digitSum(n) = n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10)

Worked examples:

1234                 -> 10
9                    -> 9
1000                 -> 1
0                    -> 0
-12                  -> INVALID

    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << digitSum(n) << '\n';

int digitSum(int n) {
    if (n == 0) {
        return 1;
    }
    return n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10);
}
evens and odds (from Lab 4)lab5Bd q6

Ticket numbers are typed in; how many are even and how many odd?

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

Input: count followed by count whole numbers. count is between 1 and 10; the template already reads everything into int values[10] and rejects a bad count.

ConditionPrint
count is not 1 to 10INVALID
anything elseeven odd, one space between

How to do it. Two counters come back through the reference parameters, so the function must set both to 0 before the loop — it cannot assume main did. Then one pass over count elements, adding to one counter or the other. main prints the two variables afterwards.

The arithmetic.

even = number of values with values[i] % 2 == 0
odd  = count - even

Worked examples:

6 12 7 8 15 20 3     -> 3 3

4 2 4 6 8            -> 4 0
1 0                  -> 1 0
11 2 4               -> INVALID
Starter file q6.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bd, question 6: evens and odds (from Lab 4)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

int main() {
    int count = 0;
    std::cin >> count;
    if (count < 1 || count > 10) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }
    int values[10] = {};
    for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        std::cin >> values[i];
    }

    int even = 0;
    int odd = 0;
    countEvenOdd(values, count, even, odd);
    std::cout << even << ' ' << odd << '\n';
}

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd) {
    even = 0;
    odd = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i <= count; ++i) {
        if (values[i] % 2 == 0) {
            ++even;
        } else {
            ++odd;
        }
    }
}
over-current protection (from Lab 1)lab5Be q1

Input: current safeLimit stopFlag (a current, the safe limit, and 1 when the emergency stop is pressed, 0 when it is not).

Test the conditions in this order — exceptional case first:

ConditionPrint
the current is negativeINVALID
the emergency stop is pressed, or the current is above safeLimitTRIP
the current is above 90% of safeLimitWARNING
anything elseNORMAL

The order is the whole point. A negative reading is meaningless, so it is reported before anything else is even considered — including the stop button.

Use else if for the middle conditions, so that reaching one means every condition above it was already false. Watch the boundaries: above the limit trips, exactly at it does not.

3 10 0    -> NORMAL
9.5 10 0  -> WARNING
12 10 0   -> TRIP

what kind of triangle (from Lab 2)lab5Be q2

Input: a b c, the three side lengths.

ConditionPrint
the three lengths cannot form a triangleNOT A TRIANGLE
all three sides are equalEQUILATERAL
exactly two sides are equalISOSCELES
anything elseSCALENE

How to do it. Decide whether it is a triangle at all before deciding what kind. Three lengths form a triangle only when every side is positive and each side is shorter than the other two added together — all three of those sums have to be checked, not just one. Once that is settled, compare the sides: all three equal is equilateral, otherwise any one matching pair is isosceles, and if no pair matches it is scalene. Note that the equilateral test has to come first, because all three equal also satisfies 'two are equal'.

The arithmetic.

a triangle needs  a > 0,  b > 0,  c > 0
and  a + b > c,  a + c > b,  b + c > a
equilateral  when  a = b = c
isosceles  when  exactly one of  a = b,  b = c,  a = c  holds

Worked examples:

3 3 3        -> EQUILATERAL
5 5 8        -> ISOSCELES
3 4 5        -> SCALENE

    int seconds = 0;
    splitSeconds(total, minutes, seconds);
    std::cout << minutes << ' ' << seconds << '\n';
}

void splitSeconds(int total, int& minutes, int& seconds) {
    minutes = total / 60;
    seconds = total - minutes;
}
is it a multiple? (from Lab 1)lab5Bf q1

Input: value divisor.

ConditionPrint
divisor is zeroINVALID
value is an exact multiple of divisorDIVISIBLE
anything elseNOT DIVISIBLE

value % divisor is the remainder left after dividing, so a remainder of zero means it divided exactly.

% is undefined when the divisor is zero — the program may do anything at all, including crash. So the zero has to be ruled out before the % is reached. Test it first, or let && stop early:

if (divisor != 0 && value % divisor == 0)

The left side is checked first, and if it is false the right side never runs.

Zero is a multiple of everything, and negative values work the same way — check both against your code rather than guessing.

12 4 -> DIVISIBLE
13 4 -> NOT DIVISIBLE
7 0  -> INVALID

the greatest common divisor (from Lab 2)lab5Bf q2

Input: a b, two whole numbers.

ConditionPrint
a or b is below 1INVALID
anything elsethe greatest common divisor of a and b

How to do it. Use repeated subtraction. While the two numbers differ, take the smaller away from the larger and keep both; the pair shrinks but shares exactly the divisors it started with. When they finally meet, that common value is the greatest common divisor. The branch that decides which one to subtract from lives inside the loop. Equal numbers are already the answer, so the loop must be able to run zero times.

The arithmetic.

gcd(a, a)  =  a
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a - b, b)   when  a > b
gcd(a, b)  =  gcd(a, b - a)   when  b > a
stop when  a = b

Worked examples:

12 18        -> 6
7 13         -> 1
100 75       -> 25
Starter file q2.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bf, question 2: the greatest common divisor (from Lab 2)

// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 0;
    int b = 0;
    std::cin >> a >> b;

    if (a < 1 || b < 1) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }

    while (a != b) {
        if (a > b) {
            a = a - 1;
        } else {
            b = b - a;
        }
    }
    std::cout << a << '\n';
}
factorial (from Lab 2)lab5Bf q3

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 0 or above 12INVALID
anything elsen factorial

How to do it. Start a running product at one — not at zero, which would swallow everything — and multiply it by each whole number from two up to n in turn. Nothing above the upper limit is asked for, because 13 factorial no longer fits in an int and would silently wrap around to a wrong answer; that is why the range is rejected up front. Zero factorial is one, and the loop handles it for free by never running.

The arithmetic.

n!  =  1 * 2 * 3 * ... * n
0!  =  1
n!  =  n * (n-1)!

Worked examples:

0            -> 1
1            -> 1
5            -> 120

    for (int i = 2; i <= n; ++i) {
        product = product * i;

}

adding up a roll number's digits (from Lab 4)lab5Bf q5

A quick check adds all the digits of an id number together.

int digitSum(int n);

Input: n

ConditionPrint
n is negativeINVALID
anything elsethe sum of its digits

How to do it. No loop is allowed in this file — check.sh rejects for and while. The function calls itself: the last digit is n % 10, and the rest of the number is n / 10, which is a smaller problem of the same kind. The base case is n being 0, whose digit sum is 0. main checks the sign and prints the returned value.

The arithmetic.

digitSum(0) = 0
digitSum(n) = n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10)

Worked examples:

1234                 -> 10
9                    -> 9
1000                 -> 1
0                    -> 0
-12                  -> INVALID
Starter file q5.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bf, question 5: adding up a roll number's digits (from Lab 4)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int digitSum(int n);

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << digitSum(n) << '\n';
    }
}

int digitSum(int n) {
    if (n < 10) {
        return 0;
    }
    return n % 10 + digitSum(n / 10);
}
evens and odds (from Lab 4)lab5Bf q6

Ticket numbers are typed in; how many are even and how many odd?

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

Input: count followed by count whole numbers. count is between 1 and 10; the template already reads everything into int values[10] and rejects a bad count.

ConditionPrint
count is not 1 to 10INVALID
anything elseeven odd, one space between

How to do it. Two counters come back through the reference parameters, so the function must set both to 0 before the loop — it cannot assume main did. Then one pass over count elements, adding to one counter or the other. main prints the two variables afterwards.

The arithmetic.

even = number of values with values[i] % 2 == 0
odd  = count - even

Worked examples:

6 12 7 8 15 20 3     -> 3 3
3 1 3 5              -> 0 3
4 2 4 6 8            -> 4 0
1 0                  -> 1 0
11 2 4               -> INVALID
Starter file q6.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bf, question 6: evens and odds (from Lab 4)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

int main() {
    int count = 0;
    std::cin >> count;
    if (count < 1 || count > 10) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }
    int values[10] = {};
    for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        std::cin >> values[i];
    }

    int even = 0;
    int odd = 0;
    countEvenOdd(values, count, even, odd);
    std::cout << even << ' ' << odd << '\n';
}

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd) {
    even = 0;
    odd = 0;
    for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        if (values[i] % 2 == 1) {
            ++even;
        } else {
            ++odd;
        }
    }
}
over-current protection (from Lab 1)lab5Bg q1

Input: current safeLimit stopFlag (a current, the safe limit, and 1 when the emergency stop is pressed, 0 when it is not).

Test the conditions in this order — exceptional case first:

ConditionPrint
the current is negativeINVALID
the emergency stop is pressed, or the current is above safeLimitTRIP
the current is above 90% of safeLimitWARNING
anything elseNORMAL

The order is the whole point. A negative reading is meaningless, so it is reported before anything else is even considered — including the stop button.

Use else if for the middle conditions, so that reaching one means every condition above it was already false. Watch the boundaries: above the limit trips, exactly at it does not.

3 10 0    -> NORMAL
9.5 10 0  -> WARNING
12 10 0   -> TRIP
Starter file q1.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bg, question 1: over-current protection (from Lab 1)

// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    double current = 0.0;
    double safeLimit = 0.0;
    int stopFlag = 0;
    std::cin >> current >> safeLimit >> stopFlag;

    if (stopFlag == 1 || current > safeLimit) {
        std::cout << "TRIP" << '\n';
    } else if (current < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else if (current > 0.9 * safeLimit) {
        std::cout << "WARNING" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "NORMAL" << '\n';
    }
}
what kind of triangle (from Lab 2)lab5Bg q2

Input: a b c, the three side lengths.

ConditionPrint
the three lengths cannot form a triangleNOT A TRIANGLE
all three sides are equalEQUILATERAL
exactly two sides are equalISOSCELES
anything elseSCALENE

How to do it. Decide whether it is a triangle at all before deciding what kind. Three lengths form a triangle only when every side is positive and each side is shorter than the other two added together — all three of those sums have to be checked, not just one. Once that is settled, compare the sides: all three equal is equilateral, otherwise any one matching pair is isosceles, and if no pair matches it is scalene. Note that the equilateral test has to come first, because all three equal also satisfies 'two are equal'.

The arithmetic.

a triangle needs  a > 0,  b > 0,  c > 0
and  a + b > c,  a + c > b,  b + c > a
equilateral  when  a = b = c
isosceles  when  exactly one of  a = b,  b = c,  a = c  holds

Worked examples:

3 3 3        -> EQUILATERAL
5 5 8        -> ISOSCELES
3 4 5        -> SCALENE
Starter file q2.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bg, question 2: what kind of triangle (from Lab 2)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int a = 0;
    int b = 0;
    int c = 0;
    std::cin >> a >> b >> c;

    if (a <= 0 || b <= 0 || c <= 0 || a + b <= c || a + c <= b || b + c <= a) {
        std::cout << "NOT A TRIANGLE" << '\n';
    } else if (a == b && b == c) {
        std::cout << "EQUILATERAL" << '\n';
    } else if (a == b || b == c) {
        std::cout << "ISOSCELES" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "SCALENE" << '\n';
    }
}
is it prime (from Lab 2)lab5Bg q3

Input: n, one whole number.

ConditionPrint
n is below 2INVALID
n has a divisor other than 1 and itselfNOT PRIME
anything elsePRIME

How to do it. Try every possible divisor from two up to one below n, and remember whether any of them divided exactly. Use a flag variable set before the loop and cleared the moment a divisor is found; decide what to print after the loop has finished, from the flag. Printing inside the loop is the common mistake — a number with several divisors then prints several lines. Two is prime, and it works out correctly here because the loop never runs for it.

The arithmetic.

d divides n  when  n % d = 0
n is prime  when no d with  2 <= d <= n - 1  divides n
1 and everything below it are neither prime nor composite

Worked examples:

2            -> PRIME
9            -> NOT PRIME
97           -> PRIME
Starter file q3.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bg, question 3: is it prime (from Lab 2)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 2) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }

    bool prime = true;
    for (int d = 1; d < n; ++d) {
        if (n % d == 0) {
            prime = false;
        }
    }

    if (prime) {
        std::cout << "PRIME" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << "NOT PRIME" << '\n';
    }
}
is that a real time? (from Lab 3)lab5Bg q4
bool isValidTime(int hours, int minutes);

How to do it. This is the one question in the lab with no INVALID — every pair of numbers gets a YES or a NO, because judging the input is the question. A 24-hour clock runs from 0 to 23 hours and 0 to 59 minutes, and all four of those ends are worth testing. Join the four conditions with && and return the result.

        std::cout << "YES" << '\n';

bool isValidTime(int hours, int minutes) {

}
a pyramid of cubes (from Lab 3)lab5Bg q5
int cubeVolume(int side);
int stackVolume(int n);

Input: n.

ConditionPrint
n is less than 1INVALID
anything elsethe total volume of the stack

How to do it. The stack is a pyramid of n cubes: the one on top has side 1, the next has side 2, and the one at the bottom has side n. stackVolume runs a loop counting from 1 to n, calls cubeVolume for each cube, and adds the volumes into a running total. main calls stackVolume only — the call to cubeVolume happens inside the loop.

The arithmetic.

volume of cube k = k * k * k
total for n      = 1*1*1 + 2*2*2 + ... + n*n*n

Worked examples:

1                    -> 1
2                    -> 9
3                    -> 36
5                    -> 225
0                    -> INVALID
Starter file q5.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bg, question 5: a pyramid of cubes (from Lab 3)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

int cubeVolume(int side);
int stackVolume(int n);

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << stackVolume(n) << '\n';
    }
}

int cubeVolume(int side) {
    return side * side * side;
}

int stackVolume(int n) {
    int total = 0;
    for (int k = 1; k <= n; ++k) {
        total = total + cubeVolume(k);
    }
    return total;
}

How to do it. // IC151 — lab5Bh, question 5: adding up a roll number's digits (from Lab 4)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.

#include <iostream>

int digitSum(int n);

int main() {
    int n = 0;
    std::cin >> n;

    if (n < 0) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
    } else {
        std::cout << digitSum(n) << '\n';
    }
}

int digitSum(int n) {
    if (n == 0) {
        return 0;
    }
    return n % 10 + n / 10;
}
evens and odds (from Lab 4)lab5Bh q6

Ticket numbers are typed in; how many are even and how many odd?

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

Input: count followed by count whole numbers. count is between 1 and 10; the template already reads everything into int values[10] and rejects a bad count.

ConditionPrint
count is not 1 to 10INVALID
anything elseeven odd, one space between

How to do it. Two counters come back through the reference parameters, so the function must set both to 0 before the loop — it cannot assume main did. Then one pass over count elements, adding to one counter or the other. main prints the two variables afterwards.

The arithmetic.

even = number of values with values[i] % 2 == 0
odd  = count - even

Worked examples:

6 12 7 8 15 20 3     -> 3 3
3 1 3 5              -> 0 3
4 2 4 6 8            -> 4 0
1 0                  -> 1 0
11 2 4               -> INVALID
Starter file q6.cpp, as handed out
// IC151 — lab5Bh, question 6: evens and odds (from Lab 4)
//
// This program is complete but has ONE bug. README.md says what it must
// print. Find the line that is wrong and fix it with the smallest change.
// Do not rewrite the program: the TAs grade your diff against this file.

#include <iostream>

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd);

int main() {
    int count = 0;
    std::cin >> count;
    if (count < 1 || count > 10) {
        std::cout << "INVALID" << '\n';
        return 0;
    }
    int values[10] = {};
    for (int i = 0; i < count; ++i) {
        std::cin >> values[i];
    }

    int even = 0;
    int odd = 0;
    countEvenOdd(values, count, even, odd);
    std::cout << even << ' ' << odd << '\n';
}

void countEvenOdd(const int values[], int count, int& even, int& odd) {
    even = 0;
    odd = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i < count; ++i) {
        if (values[i] % 2 == 0) {
            ++even;
        } else {
            ++odd;
        }
    }
}

Lab 6

structs, pointers and dynamic memory · 64 different questions · 16 forms

Lab instructions (as given in lab6B1a)

Four questions, one file each. This lab covers lectures 13 and 14: an array of structs searched by a function that returns a pointer or nullptr, an array whose size is only known at run time (owned by a std::unique_ptr from std::make_unique<int[]>), and a linked list built by inserting at the head and walked until nullptr. No std::vector, no std::string.

This course uses C++17. Build any question with:

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic q1.cpp -o q1
./q1

To catch memory errors as well, build with the address sanitizer (Lecture 14):

g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra -pedantic -g -fsanitize=address q4.cpp -o q4

Each program reads its input from the keyboard and prints one line.

Every function a question names must be declared above main (the prototype, ending in a semicolon) and defined below main. check.sh looks for both, and for the shape each question asks for (q1 uses nullptr and ->; q2 uses std::make_unique<int[]> and no new or delete; q3 and q4 build a list with new Node, free it with delete, and use no array at all). A program that prints the right answer some other way scores nothing.

q3 and q4 both use this node and these two functions (declare and define them in each file):

struct Node {
    int value;
    Node* next;
};

void pushFront(Node*& head, int value);   // new Node{value, head}, then head points at it
void release(Node* head);                 // save next, delete the node, move on
